subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage: In the fifth-floor dev room of a logistics firm, Anjali, a junior developer, was rushing to clear a ticket before the evening stand-up. The AI tool wrote the search function in seconds, the tests turned green, and Anjali merged it without reading past the first lines. It felt like a small win. Three days later Sunaina, doing a routine pass over merged code, stopped at the query. It built its command by pasting user text straight into it, which left the search box open to tricks. Sunaina raised it with the team lead at once, the change was pulled, and the cleanup took two people a full day. Anjali sat very still at the stand-up. 'I just trusted that green meant fine,' she said quietly.

qa.q: How long after the merge did Sunaina notice the query?
qa.a: Sunaina noticed it three days later.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling at the stand-up?
qa.a: Anjali felt embarrassed and regretful, sitting very still and admitting a trust in green tests.

qa.q: What could Anjali do differently with AI-written code next time?
qa.a: Anjali could read every line, test odd inputs, and ask a colleague to review before merging, since passing basic tests does not prove the code is safe.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt on finding the query?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably concerned about the risk to users, which is why they raised it with the lead at once.

grounding: Shows a junior developer merging AI-written code unread, so an insecure query passes basic tests and reaches production before a reviewer notices.
